title: HyVox: Rethinking Low-Power Voice Intelligence with Hybrid Neuromorphic–von Neumann Edge Computing

paper.title: HyVox : Rethinking Low-Power Voice Intelligence with Hybrid Neuromorphic–von Neumann Edge Computing
paper.abstract:
Abstract. In this paper, we present HyVox , a hybrid neuromorphic–von Neumann system for
low-energy open-set speaker identification under extremely tight
energy budgets . HyVox splits the workload at the speaker embedding. A neuromorphic processor embeds the speech with
sparse, event-driven computation, and a von Neumann microcontroller holds the speaker gallery and makes every decision: it scores queries by
cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing
a prototype, with no weight update. On the neuromorphic processor, a
hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone learns a synaptic time
constant per leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, allocating 832 832 neurons
across fast, medium, and slow timescales. A 32 32 -neuron spiking embedding
extractor (SEE), pretrained on episodes that each enroll new speakers and
reject outsiders, turns the backbone output into an embedding for speakers
unseen in training; its 32 32 spike counts are the only interface between the
two processors. To fit the chip’s synapse and integer budgets, we compress
the backbone 6.5 × 6.5\times to 29.0 29.0 k synapses, train it for integer bit-shift
dynamics, and fine-tune it with chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). CAST
trains through a differentiable replica of the chip’s integer neuron update,
derived from its cycle-accurate simulator, so that gradient descent optimizes
the exact weights and thresholds the chip runs; it doubles the top-1 accuracy
of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers. On 20 20 Common Voice households of
unseen speakers, HyVox reaches 99.6 % 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5 % 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 2 members and 94.9 % 94.9\% and 13.2 % 13.2\% with 20 20 , and the network deployed on
the neuromorphic chip matches its trained model. Each inference on a 3 3 -s window takes 0.96 ​ s 0.96\,\mathrm{s} and 1.63 ​ mJ 1.63\,\mathrm{mJ} of dynamic energy, 42 % 42\% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5 × 13.5\times less
dynamic and 5.8 × 5.8\times less total energy than the most energy-efficient one.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Motivation. Smart audio devices are moving from fixed command recognition ( Warden, 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; Kim et al., 2021 ) toward personalized speaker identity ( Variani et al., 2014 ; Snyder et al., 2018 ; Gallacher et al., 2023 ) . A shared smart speaker adds household members after it is installed, a hearable recognizes its owner, and a home appliance tailors its responses to the enrolled user who speaks and treats strangers as guests. In each case the speakers that matter are defined after deployment ( Snell et al., 2017 ; Wan et al., 2018 ) : the device enrolls a new user from a short recording, keeps that user’s representation in local memory, compares every query against a gallery that changes over time, and rejects speech from anyone who is not enrolled ( Scheirer et al., 2013 ; Geng et al., 2021 ; Vaze et al., 2022 ) . These operations run on battery-powered hardware, so the energy of the inference that turns a window of speech into speaker evidence bounds how many decisions the device can make on one charge ( David et al., 2021 ; Banbury et al., 2021 ; Yik et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1 . HyVox ’s concept: Hybrid platform for low-energy speaker identification Current Approaches and Limitations. Speaker identification on edge devices runs as a TinyML pipeline on a von Neumann microcontroller. A compact artificial neural network (ANN), such as DS-CNN ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , BC-ResNet ( Kim et al., 2021 ) , or the small-footprint speaker network of Balian et al. ( Balian et al., 2021 ) , embeds each window of audio, and the same microcontroller scores the embedding against a gallery of enrolled prototypes, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users. Scoring takes only a few dot products per enrolled speaker, so ANN inference accounts for nearly all of the energy of a decision. On a von Neumann core, each multiply–accumulate of this inference fetches its weight and activation from memory, so this data movement sets the energy of every inference. Neuromorphic processors such as Xylo Audio 3 ( SynSense, 2023 ) remove this traffic: an event-driven front end and spiking cores keep weights beside the neurons and compute only when spikes arrive. A neuromorphic core running a spiking neural network (SNN) is therefore a natural replacement for the ANN in the TinyML pipeline. Moving the entire open-set pipeline onto the neuromorphic core, however, is infeasible. The core executes only the SNN mapped onto it and has no general-purpose compute, so it cannot store a gallery that changes at runtime, normalize and compare embeddings, apply a rejection threshold, or enroll a speaker without reconfiguring the network. Existing neuromorphic audio work ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; Bos and Muir, 2024 ) accordingly targets closed-set classification and keyword spotting. The same co-location that saves energy also caps the network size: every weight occupies on-chip memory beside its neuron, so Xylo Audio 3 holds at most 1,000 1{,}000 spiking neurons and 31,744 31{,}744 int8 recurrent synapses, orders of magnitude below the millions of parameters of standard speaker encoders ( Snyder et al., 2018 ) . Two questions remain open: how to learn a speaker embedding that generalizes to unseen speakers within this fixed hardware budget, and how to design a system that combines the low-energy inference of a neuromorphic chip with the general-purpose compute that open-set recognition requires. Proposed Approach. In this paper, we present HyVox , a hybrid neuromorphic–von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification (Fig. 1 ). The central idea is to split the workload at the embedding: the neuromorphic core takes over the ANN’s role in the TinyML pipeline, and the von Neumann microcontroller (MCU) keeps every operation that needs general-purpose compute. Xylo Audio 3 runs the audio front end (AFE) and a spiking embedding network and emits one 32-component spike-count vector per inference on a three-second window. An STM32L476 MCU host turns these counts into decisions: it holds a gallery of speaker prototypes, scores each query by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing a prototype. The spiking network is shared by every device and never trained on a user’s audio; each household differs only in the gallery on its host. Challenges. Moving the embedding from an ANN on the MCU to an SNN on the neuromorphic core places the whole burden of recognition on a network of fixed size, integer dynamics, and a 32 32 -neuron output, and that output must still support every open-set decision the MCU makes. This raises four challenges, from the design of the network to its execution on the chip: • Speaker evidence in a small SNN. Speaker evidence spans milliseconds (formant transitions, plosive releases) to hundreds of milliseconds (pitch contour, speaking rate). ANN encoders cover this range with depth and width, but the chip holds 1,000 1{,}000 neurons. In a spiking network the only memory of the past is each neuron’s decay, so the timescales assigned to so few neurons determine which speaker evidence the network can represent at all. • A 32 32 -dimensional spiking embedding for unseen speakers. The chip’s hidden state never leaves the chip; the MCU receives only the spike count of each of the 32 32 readout neurons per window. These counts are the entire interface, so they must serve directly as the embedding: they must identify speakers absent from training, enroll a new speaker from one minute of speech with no weight update, and separate speakers who were never enrolled so the MCU can reject them. Large-corpus pretraining separates a fixed set of training speakers and never practises enrollment or rejection. • Fitting the hardware’s synapse and precision budget. On-chip memory bounds the number of synapses; Xylo Audio 3 holds at most 31,744 31{,}744 . A fully connected network of five layers of width w w has four connections between adjacent layers of w 2 w^{2} synapses each, so the budget allows w ≈ 31,744 / 4 ≈ 89 w\approx\sqrt{31{,}744/4}\approx 89 , about 445 445 neurons in total. That is under half of Xylo’s 1,000 1{,}000 and too few to cover the timescales of speaker evidence. A network with enough neurons exceeds the synapse budget several times over and must lose most of its synapses to fit, and the hardware further restricts weights to low-precision integers and decays to a discrete set, int8 weights and power-of-two bit shifts on Xylo. Each of these steps removes speaker information that training must recover. • The gap between the trained network and the chip. Even after compression and quantization, the chip computes differently from the model used in training. On the chip, a neuron can fire only a limited number of times per timestep, signals take extra timesteps to pass from one layer to the next, and neuron state is clipped when it exceeds the register range. Training ignores all three, so the network learns to rely on behavior the chip cannot reproduce, and a network that recognizes speakers well in training can lose much of its accuracy once it runs on the chip. Technical Contributions. HyVox addresses these challenges with four matching contributions: • HTA-SNN backbone. We design a hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone of 832 832 leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons that learns a synaptic time constant per neuron, so training allocates the neuron budget across timescales, with cross-scale projections that carry fast acoustic evidence to the slow stages (Sec. 4 ). At the same synapse budget, it exceeds SynNet ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; Bos and Muir, 2024 ) , the reference SNN for Xylo, by 4.1 4.1 top-1 points and 1.6 1.6 equal error rate (EER) points. • Spiking embedding extractor (SEE). We propose a 32 32 -neuron spiking readout pretrained episodically on speakers disjoint from the backbone’s: every episode enrolls new speakers from a few windows and rejects speakers who are not enrolled (Sec. 5 ). Its normalized spike counts are the trained embedding, so the STM32 host holds every speaker-specific quantity, the gallery, a sliding three-window buffer, and a threshold per gallery size, enrolls a user with forward passes and a prototype write, and decides in under 10 3 10^{3} operations with 64 64 bytes per speaker, one signed 16-bit value per embedding dimension (Sec. 6.5 ). • Dense-to-sparse compression. Since a large sparse network outperforms a small dense one with the same number of weights ( Zhu and Gupta, 2017 ) , we train the backbone dense, with 188.4 188.4 k synapses ( 5.9 × 5.9\times the budget), and compress it 6.5 × 6.5\times to 29.0 29.0 k synapses, 15.4 % 15.4\% of the dense network, on a 293 293 -timestep task. To achieve this, we extend SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) , whose Fisher spike contribution scores channels and was demonstrated on a 4 4 -timestep image classifier at a single pruning ratio, to a per-synapse score ranked globally across stages and skip connections, and prune iteratively in 14 14 steps while the learned time constants settle onto the chip’s bit-shift grid (Sec. 6.1 ). Training the compressed network for the chip’s integer bitshift dynamics then recovers its accuracy before quantization (Secs. 6.2 and 7.7 ). • Chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). We derive a trainable PyTorch replica of the chip’s integer neuron update from the chip’s cycle-accurate simulator and fine-tune the network through it, a method that applies to any digital neuromorphic chip with such a simulator. Our CAST replica for Xylo reproduces 99.8 % 99.8\% of the simulator’s hidden spike counts exactly. Its trainable parameters are the chip’s own int8 weights and integer thresholds, so gradient descent optimizes the configuration the chip runs, under its event limits and per-layer delay. CAST doubles the top-1 of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers, from 31 % 31\% to 61 % 61\% (Sec. 7.7 ). We evaluate HyVox on 20 20 accent-homogeneous Common Voice households of speakers unseen by both the backbone and the SEE. HyVox reaches 99.6 % 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5 % 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 2 members and 94.9 % 94.9\% and 13.2 % 13.2\% with 20 20 . On 20 20 further households, the deployed system on the chip matches or exceeds the PyTorch model it was fine-tuned from, with 96.7 % 96.7\% top-1 and 10.0 % 10.0\% EER at n = 20 n=20 . HyVox reduces the inference energy. Each inference on a three-second window takes 0.96 ​ s 0.96\,\mathrm{s} and 1.63 ​ mJ 1.63\,\mathrm{mJ} of dynamic energy, 13.5 × 13.5\times less dynamic and 5.8 × 5.8\times less total energy than the most energy-efficient embedded ANN baseline, with a 42 % 42\% lower latency than the fastest one.

sections.heading: 2. Background
sections.text: This section covers speaker embeddings and how TinyML pipelines compute them on embedded devices, spiking neural networks (SNNs) and the neuromorphic processors that run them, and how a trained SNN is fitted to neuromorphic hardware. Speaker embeddings and the TinyML pipeline. Speaker recognition is commonly framed as an embedding problem: an encoder maps each utterance to a vector whose geometry places same-speaker examples close together and different-speaker examples far apart ( Variani et al., 2014 ; Snyder et al., 2018 ) . Angular-margin classification ( Deng et al., 2019 ) learns this geometry from a large set of labelled training speakers, and supervised contrastive learning ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) shapes it directly over pairs of examples. In open-set recognition the deployed speakers are not known at training time ( Geng et al., 2021 ; Vaze et al., 2022 ) : the device enrolls each user as a normalized prototype ( Snell et al., 2017 ) , scores a query against every prototype by cosine similarity, and rejects the query when its best score falls below a threshold. Few-shot open-set learning ( Liu et al., 2020 ; C et al., 2022 ) trains for this use. Each training episode samples a new set of speakers, builds their prototypes from a few examples, classifies further examples of them, and includes speakers outside the set that must be rejected, so the model practises enrollment and rejection on speakers that change in every episode. On an edge device, the whole pipeline runs on one microcontroller ( David et al., 2021 ; Banbury et al., 2021 ) . A compact artificial neural network, such as DS-CNN ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , BC-ResNet ( Kim et al., 2021 ) , or the speaker network of Balian et al. ( Balian et al., 2021 ) , computes the embedding from frame-level features such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), and the same core stores the gallery, scores, and enrolls. Spiking neural networks and neuromorphic processors. Neuromorphic audio systems encode sound as sparse events and process them with a spiking neural network (SNN) of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons ( Gerstner and Kistler, 2002 ) . Each neuron’s synaptic current and membrane voltage decay with time constants τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} and τ mem \tau_{\mathrm{mem}} , and the neuron spikes when its voltage crosses a threshold. These decays are a feed-forward SNN’s only memory of past input, so they set how far back each neuron integrates acoustic evidence. Surrogate gradients carry training through the non-differentiable spike ( Neftci et al., 2019 ) . Neuromorphic processors ( Akopyan et al., 2015 ; Davies et al., 2018 ; Bos and Muir, 2023 ) store each weight beside its neuron and compute only when spikes arrive ( Roy et al., 2019 ) , so the silicon fixes the size and arithmetic of the network. In Xylo Audio 3 ( SynSense, 2023 ) , an audio front end converts the microphone signal into a 16 16 -channel spike raster for its spiking core. Its limits are typical of the class: at most 1,000 1{,}000 hidden neurons and 31,744 31{,}744 int8 recurrent synapses; integer thresholds and 16 16 -bit saturating state; power-of-two decays; at most 31 31 events per hidden neuron and one per readout neuron per timestep; 32 32 readout neurons as the only off-chip output; and one timestep of delay per hidden-to-hidden hop. Fitting a trained network to neuromorphic hardware. Deploying an SNN trained in floating point on a neuromorphic chip involves three steps: pruning, quantization-aware training, and mapping. Pruning removes synapses until the network meets the synapse budget; at a fixed number of weights, pruning a large dense network yields higher accuracy than training a small dense one ( Zhu and Gupta, 2017 ) , and SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) adapts compression-aware fine-tuning to SNNs, pruning the channels with the lowest Fisher spike contribution. Quantization-aware training (QAT) ( Jacob et al., 2018 ) simulates the chip’s integer weights and bit-shift decays in the forward pass and passes gradients through the rounding with the straight-through estimator ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) . Mapping converts the trained parameters into the chip configuration, and a cycle-accurate simulator, such as XyloSim in Rockpool ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ) , predicts the spikes the chip will produce.

sections.heading: 3. System Overview
sections.text: HyVox splits open-set speaker identification at the embedding. A spiking network on Xylo Audio 3 embeds each three-second window of audio, and an STM32L476 host keeps every operation that needs general-purpose compute. Fig. 2 shows the two parts of the system: an offline pipeline that trains the spiking network and fits it to the chip (right), and the hybrid neuromorphic audio platform that runs it on the device (left). Our four contributions form the offline pipeline. The HTA-SNN backbone and the SEE define the network, and dense-to-sparse compression and CAST fit it to the chip. The neuromorphic–von Neumann platform then runs the network, with the open-set gallery on the host. Figure 2 . HyVox system overview: offline training and mapping (right) and the inference pipeline (left).

sections.heading: 3.1. Model Training and Mapping
sections.text: HTA-SNN backbone. The backbone is a hierarchical temporal abstraction SNN of 832 832 LIF neurons that learns a synaptic time constant per neuron and carries fast acoustic evidence to its slow stages through cross-scale projections (Sec. 4 ). It is pretrained as a speaker classifier on VoxCeleb2 from the 16 16 -channel spike rasters of the chip’s audio front end (AFE), so the network learns from the same input it receives on the device. Dense-to-sparse compression. The backbone is trained dense with 188.4 188.4 k synapses, 5.9 × 5.9\times the chip’s budget. Our per-synapse extension of SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) then prunes it iteratively to 29.0 29.0 k synapses with compression-aware fine-tuning (Sec. 6.1 ), and quantization-aware training replaces the floating-point LIF update with the chip’s int8 weights and bit-shift decays (Sec. 6.2 ). Chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). The quantized backbone still runs without the chip’s event caps and per-hop delay. CAST fine-tunes it through a PyTorch replica of the chip’s integer neuron update, derived from the cycle-accurate simulator XyloSim, whose trainable parameters are the chip’s own int8 weights and integer thresholds. Training therefore optimizes the exact configuration that is written to the chip (Sec. 6.3 ). Spiking embedding extractor (SEE). With the backbone frozen, the SEE, a 32 32 -neuron spiking readout, is pretrained episodically on VoxCeleb1, whose speakers are disjoint from the backbone’s VoxCeleb2 speakers. Each episode enrolls new speakers from a few windows, identifies further windows of them, and rejects speakers who are not enrolled, so the readout learns the operations the device later performs on its users (Sec. 5 ). The SEE is finally fine-tuned on the chip-exact spikes of the CAST backbone. The backbone and the SEE are mapped once to a single Xylo configuration that serves every device; no weight is ever trained on a user’s audio.

sections.heading: 3.2. Hybrid Neuromorphic Audio Platform
sections.text: Neuromorphic core. A 16 ​ kHz 16\,\mathrm{kHz} microphone feeds the AFE of Xylo Audio 3, which converts the waveform into a 16 16 -channel spike raster. Each three-second window of this raster drives the mapped HTA-SNN and SEE from a reset state, and the chip emits the spike counts of the 32 32 SEE neurons. This count vector is the only output of the chip and the entire interface to the host. Hybrid manager. The firmware’s hybrid manager mediates the chip–host boundary. A cycle scheduler issues a read trigger at the end of each window, the readout transfers the 32 32 counts over UART, and a mode controller sets the host to enrollment or identification. One decision moves 70 70 bytes per three-second window, independent of the size of the network on the chip. von Neumann core. The STM32 runs the metric kernel and holds every speaker-specific quantity. It L2-normalizes each count vector into the trained embedding, averages the latest three windows, scores the result against every prototype in the gallery by cosine similarity, and accepts the best match only if its score reaches a rejection threshold chosen for the current gallery size. In enrollment mode, the host accumulates the normalized embeddings of a new speaker’s windows into one prototype and writes it to the gallery. Adding or deleting a speaker is a write to host memory with 64 64 bytes per speaker, and the network on the chip is unchanged, so each household differs from another only in the gallery on its host (Sec. 6.5 ).

sections.heading: 4. Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction (HTA)
sections.text: Speaker identity includes multiple temporal scales: short-timescale acoustic events (plosive releases, formant transitions, fricative onsets) cue vocal-tract structure, while longer patterns (speaking rate, pitch contour, slowly varying resonance) give more stable evidence over hundreds of milliseconds. Modern encoders capture this range with deep, over-parameterised temporal models ( Snyder et al., 2018 ; Desplanques et al., 2020 ) , but current neuromorphic hardware, including Xylo Audio 3 ( SynSense, 2023 ) , caps the deployed network at 1,000 1{,}000 neurons, 31,744 31{,}744 recurrent synapses, and low-precision integer weights. Naively reducing conventional architectures to this regime strips precisely the temporal capacity needed for robust discrimination; the architectural problem is thus not just fewer neurons, but allocating the remaining state to the right timescales. To overcome this, we propose hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA), a compact LIF hierarchy for speaker embeddings. Its layers learn distinct integration windows, allowing fast acoustic cues and slower speaker patterns to be represented in the same model. Cross-scale projections carry short-timescale evidence forward while deeper layers accumulate long-range speaker context.

sections.heading: 4.1. HTA’s Concept
sections.text: Our key observation is that the temporal depth in a spiking network is not determined only by the number of layers, but also by the temporal filtering applied before each neuron integrates its input. Hence, we distinguish the two LIF timescales explicitly. The membrane time constant τ mem \tau_{\mathrm{mem}} controls how long a neuron retains voltage after receiving current; in our model it is fixed at 2 2 timesteps for every neuron. The synaptic time constant τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} controls the temporal content delivered to the membrane by filtering presynaptic spike trains. This is the trainable quantity in HTA. Small τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} values preserve sharp transients, while larger τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} values expose the neuron to evidence integrated over longer intervals ( Gerstner and Kistler, 2002 ) . Our backbone instead reuses a single stream of spiking state: early layers form fast local descriptors, intermediate layers integrate over broader acoustic patterns, and deeper layers accumulate speaker-level context. Cross-scale skip projections then expose early detail to later integrators without introducing a full parallel pathway.

sections.heading: 4.2.2. Cross-Scale Fusion
sections.text: A strictly feed-forward temporal hierarchy creates a failure mode i.e. fast phonetic evidence must pass through progressively slower layers before it can affect the embedding. By the time it reaches the readout, transient structure may have been attenuated by repeated integration. HTA mitigates this bottleneck with two projected skip connections. The first injects the input projection 𝐡 1 \mathbf{h}_{1} into the long-range integrator, giving the global layer access to unsmoothed spectral evidence. The second injects the local representation 𝐡 2 \mathbf{h}_{2} into the readout integrator, preserving short-timescale articulatory cues alongside deeper context vector. These skips are not residual blocks in the conventional deep-network sense, they connect different channel widths and different temporal regimes. Their role is cross-scale fusion under a fixed neuron budget. The final embedding therefore reflects three complementary sources of information i.e. fast local events from early layers, intermediate acoustic trajectories, and long-range speaker context from the deeper integrators.

sections.heading: 4.2.3. Hardware Compliance
sections.text: The backbone contains 64 + 128 + 256 + 256 + 128 = 832 64+128+256+256+128=832 LIF neurons, within Xylo’s 1,000 1{,}000 hidden neurons, and the SEE (Sec. 5 ) occupies the chip’s 32 32 readout neurons. The final 128-neuron backbone layer also respects the constraint that the layer driving the hardware readout interface must not exceed 128 neurons. The architecture therefore fits the chip in its neuron count, its readout width, and its integer spike-rate pooling, and the embedding comes from the 32 32 readout neurons, the only neurons whose spikes leave the chip during deployment.

sections.heading: 5. Spiking Embedding Extractor (SEE)
sections.text: Pretrained on VoxCeleb2 (Sec. 4 ), the HTA backbone has learned to extract features that distinguish one speaker from another. However, it learns them as a closed-set classifier, separating a fixed set of training speakers, whereas the deployed system faces an open-set problem. Its users are never part of training: a user is enrolled on the device from a short enrollment recording (Sec. 5.3 ), and no network weight is updated with that audio. In operation the device also hears guests who were never enrolled. The system must therefore recognise an enrolled speaker from a representation built from that recording and turn away audio from anyone else. Closed-set training exercises neither requirement: the classifier never builds a speaker representation from a few examples, and never encounters speakers outside its training set, whose voices may fall anywhere between the learned classes. Open-set recognition thus calls for an embedding extractor that has learned, from other speakers, how to separate speakers given only a few shots each, and how to separate them from speakers who are not enrolled. To this end, we propose the spiking embedding extractor (SEE), a 32-neuron spiking readout on top of the frozen backbone. The SEE is trained episodically on a disjoint speaker corpus: each episode enrolls a new set of training speakers from a few windows, identifies further windows of those speakers, and rejects speakers who are not enrolled, the same operations the deployed system later performs on its users without any further training.

sections.heading: 5.1. SEE’s Concept
sections.text: Our key observation is that, once the backbone is fixed, recognizing a speaker on the device takes three steps in one embedding space: average a speaker’s enrollment embeddings into a prototype, find the prototype closest to a query by cosine similarity, and reject the query if that similarity is below a threshold. The SEE is trained to produce embeddings for exactly these steps, so the network used at inference is the network trained, with no classifier or scoring layer added. Let f θ f_{\theta} denote the frozen HTA backbone. For an AFE spike raster 𝐱 ∈ ℤ T × 16 \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{T\times 16} , the backbone emits the spike sequence f θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) = [ 𝐳 1 , … , 𝐳 T ] f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=[\mathbf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{T}] with 𝐳 t ∈ { 0 , 1 } 128 \mathbf{z}_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{128} . We write E ⁡ ( ⋅ ) E(\cdot) for the full extractor, i.e. , the backbone and the SEE together. The normalised spike count is identical to the normalised mean spike rate and to the integer count vector read from Xylo (Sec. 6.5 ). Spike counts are non-negative, so every 𝐫 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{r}} lies in the positive orthant and the windows of any two speakers share a large common component. Subtracting 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} , the mean of 𝐫 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{r}} over training windows, removes this component, so cosine similarities reflect what distinguishes one speaker from another. This design keeps the learning problem deliberately small. The backbone carries the speaker-discriminative structure learned from VoxCeleb2, and the SEE learns only how to expose that structure in 32 dimensions so that the same-speaker windows fall close to their prototype, different speakers fall apart, and unenrolled speakers stay away from every prototype. Because the SEE never encodes which speakers are enrolled, the identities it serves can change after training without changing the network.

sections.text: We pretrain the SEE for two properties: generalization to speakers that were never seen in training, and rejection of speakers that are not enrolled. Both follow from few-shot open-set learning (FSOSL) ( C et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2020 ) , in which the model is trained on episodes that each simulate one enrollment scenario. In each episode, we select N N speakers with K K support windows and Q Q query windows per speaker, an N N -way K K -shot problem. The support windows play the role of enrollment utterances, and the prototype of speaker k k is the normalised mean of its support embeddings, (16) 𝐜 k = ∑ 𝐱 ∈ 𝒮 k E ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ‖ ∑ 𝐱 ∈ 𝒮 k E ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) ‖ 2 , \small\mathbf{c}_{k}=\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{S}_{k}}E(\mathbf{x})}{\left\|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{S}_{k}}E(\mathbf{x})\right\|_{2}}, where 𝒮 k ⊂ 𝒮 seen \mathcal{S}_{k}\subset\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{seen}} holds the support windows of speaker k k . sections.heading: 5.4. Runtime Enrollment using SEE
sections.text: Runtime enrollment adds a speaker to the gallery without modifying the network. Because the SEE was pretrained on episodes that each enroll a new set of speakers, runtime enrollment performs the same operation as every training episode, applied to a speaker the SEE has never seen. No gradient step, fine-tuning, or reflashing of Xylo is required. For a new speaker k new k_{\mathrm{new}} , the device records the enrollment speech, Xylo embeds each window with the fixed backbone and SEE, and the host computes 𝐜 k new \mathbf{c}_{k_{\mathrm{new}}} from these embeddings exactly as in Sec. 5.3 . The prototype is then appended to the gallery, (23) 𝒢 ← 𝒢 ∪ { ( k new , 𝐜 k new ) } . \small\mathcal{G}\leftarrow\mathcal{G}\cup\{(k_{\mathrm{new}},\mathbf{c}_{k_{\mathrm{new}}})\}. The prototypes of the existing speakers are not recomputed, so enrollment order does not matter and adding one speaker never disturbs another. The next query is scored against the updated gallery, and the new speaker is both identified and defended against guests by the same threshold as every other member. Removing a speaker is the inverse operation, deleting its prototype. Enrollment therefore costs only the forward passes over the enrollment windows and one 32-dimensional write to host memory; its STM32 implementation is described in Sec. 6.5 . The pretrained SEE is shared by every deployment. Two devices with different households run identical networks and differ only in their galleries. The network is retrained and reflashed only if the backbone or SEE itself is updated, in which case every stored prototype belongs to the previous embedding space and all speakers are re-enrolled.

sections.heading: 6. Chip-Accurate Training for Neuromorphic Deployment
sections.text: The pretrained HTA-SNN and SEE (Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 ) are floating-point networks. Xylo Audio 3 runs a different network: 31,744 31{,}744 int8 recurrent synapses, integer thresholds, power-of-two decays, at most 31 31 events per hidden neuron and timestep, one timestep of delay per hidden-to-hidden hop, and 16 16 -bit saturating state. Each of these limits removes speaker information, and the last three are invisible to any model that does not compute exactly as the chip does. We close this gap in four steps (Fig. 2 , right). Dense-to-sparse compression fits the synapse budget (Sec. 6.1 ), bitshift quantization-aware training fits the integer dynamics (Sec. 6.2 ), and chip-accurate spiking training (CAST), which trains through a replica of the chip, fits the event limits, hop delays, and saturation (Sec. 6.3 ). The SEE is then fine-tuned through the CAST replica’s readout on the spikes the chip produces (Sec. 6.4 ). The three backbone steps train on VoxCeleb2, the backbone’s pretraining data, and the SEE fine-tuning trains on the VoxCeleb1 training speakers of the SEE’s pretraining (Sec. 5.2 ). Every step starts from the model of the step before, so the network that reaches the chip is the network that was trained for it.

sections.heading: 6.1. Dense-to-Sparse Compression
sections.text: At a fixed number of weights, a large sparse network outperforms a small dense one ( Zhu and Gupta, 2017 ) , and the HTA backbone needs its 832 832 neurons to cover the timescales of speaker evidence (Sec. 4 ). We therefore train the backbone dense, with 188.4 188.4 k synapses, 5.9 × 5.9\times the chip’s budget, and compress it by extending SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) . SpikeFit removes whole channels, and its authors evaluate it at a single pruning ratio on an image classifier that runs for 4 4 timesteps ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) . In our case, the chip’s budget counts individual synapses, and our backbone runs for 293 293 timesteps and must lose 84.6 % 84.6\% of its synapses, so we lift SpikeFit’s channel score to a per-synapse score, rank it globally across stages and skip connections, and prune iteratively. SpikeFit scores each neuron c c by its Fisher spike contribution, (24) F c = 1 N ​ ∑ b , t ( ∂ ℒ ∂ y b , t , c ) 2 ​ y b , t , c 2 , \small F_{c}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{b,t}\Bigl(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y_{b,t,c}}\Bigr)^{2}y_{b,t,c}^{2}, where y b , t , c y_{b,t,c} is the neuron’s spike output on calibration window b b at timestep t t and ℒ \mathcal{L} is the AAM-Softmax pretraining loss. We extend this score to synapses. A synapse from neuron j j to neuron i i receives the score | W i ​ j | ​ a j ​ F i |W_{ij}|\,a_{j}\,F_{i} , where W i ​ j W_{ij} is its weight and a j a_{j} is the firing rate of the presynaptic neuron, so a synapse survives when it is strong, carries spikes, and feeds a neuron that matters to the loss. Synapses are ranked across all layers and removed in 14 14 steps, each followed by compression-aware fine-tuning. This fine-tuning, SpikeFit’s clusterization-aware training ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) , gives every layer a codebook of 256 256 learnable weight values, initialized by k-means on the layer’s weights, so each weight can be stored as an 8-bit index. In the forward pass every weight is replaced by its nearest codebook value, gradients reach the full-precision weight through the straight-through estimator ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) , and a commitment loss, the mean squared distance between each weight and its codebook value, moves every codebook value toward the weights assigned to it. The global ranking lets each stage keep the synapses it needs, so the network decides where its budget goes. The result has 29.0 29.0 k synapses, 6.5 × 6.5\times fewer than the dense backbone. Before the last pruning step, every learned time constant is snapped to the chip’s bit-shift grid and frozen, (25) d syn = round ⁡ ( log 2 ⁡ τ syn ) , τ ^ syn = 2 d syn , \small d_{\mathrm{syn}}=\operatorname{round}\bigl(\log_{2}\tau_{\mathrm{syn}}\bigr),\hskip 18.49988pt\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{syn}}=2^{d_{\mathrm{syn}}}, where τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} is in timesteps and d syn d_{\mathrm{syn}} is the integer bit shift that the chip stores per neuron, clipped to its range 1 ≤ d syn ≤ 8 1\leq d_{\mathrm{syn}}\leq 8 . Each timestep, the chip decays the synaptic current I I by I ← I − ⌊ I / 2 d syn ⌋ I\leftarrow I-\lfloor I/2^{d_{\mathrm{syn}}}\rfloor , which approximates an exponential decay with time constant 2 d syn 2^{d_{\mathrm{syn}}} . The final fine-tuning recovers accuracy under the timescales the chip will run, and the learned allocation of fast, medium, and slow neurons carries over to the chip.

sections.heading: 6.2. Bitshift Quantization-Aware Training
sections.text: The chip decays both the synaptic current and the membrane voltage with the integer bit shift x ← x − ⌊ x / 2 d ⌋ x\leftarrow x-\lfloor x/2^{d}\rfloor , where d ∈ { d syn , d mem } d\in\{d_{\mathrm{syn}},d_{\mathrm{mem}}\} is the shift of the decaying state. This update differs from the floating-point update x ← ( 1 − 2 − d ) ​ x x\leftarrow(1-2^{-d})\,x by its rounding at every timestep, and these rounding errors accumulate over the 293 293 timesteps of a window. Bitshift quantization-aware training replaces the floating-point LIF update of every neuron with this integer update, passes gradients through the rounding with the straight-through estimator ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) , and fine-tunes the compressed backbone with the AAM-Softmax objective. The result is a backbone whose weights, decays, and state updates are all integer.

sections.heading: 6.3. Chip-Accurate Spiking Training (CAST)
sections.text: The remaining gap. After bitshift QAT the backbone uses the chip’s integer arithmetic, but three chip limits are still absent from training: the hop delays of the chip’s recurrent layout, the per-timestep event caps, and 16-bit state saturation. Training updates the backbone as a stack of layers within one timestep. Xylo runs the hidden neurons as one recurrent population with a single shared weight matrix, so the skip projections of HTA are folded into direct synapses (Sec. 7.7 gives the resulting synapse count) and every hidden-to-hidden hop costs one timestep. Skip A reaches the global stage in one hop and the main path in three, and likewise for skip B into the readout stage, so evidence that training adds at the same timestep arrives on the chip two timesteps apart. Each hidden neuron emits at most 31 31 events per timestep, each input channel carries at most 15 15 events per bin, and the synaptic current and membrane voltage saturate at 16 16 bits. A network trained without these limits learns to rely on dynamics the chip cannot reproduce, and mapped directly to the chip, the QAT backbone loses half of its top-1 accuracy (Sec. 7.7 ). Imposing the event caps in the training model alone does not close this gap, since the delays, the folded skips, and the integer mapping still move every neuron. Training therefore has to see the chip’s computation itself. The CAST replica. The chip’s cycle-accurate simulator, XyloSim, reproduces this computation but provides no gradients. We propose chip-accurate spiking training (CAST), which trains the backbone through a differentiable PyTorch replica of the chip’s neuron update, with the update rule derived from XyloSim. Hardware-in-the-loop training runs the forward pass on the chip and computes gradients through a software model of it ( Schmitt et al., 2017 ; Cramer et al., 2022 ) . It suits analog chips such as BrainScaleS-2, whose device mismatch no simulator reproduces. A digital neuromorphic chip computes deterministically, so CAST replaces the chip with a software replica of its integer update. Training then needs no hardware, runs at GPU speed on millions of windows, and computes its gradients through the same arithmetic as its forward pass. The training tools that accompany digital chips, such as the Rockpool library for Xylo ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ) , model individual constraints on a layered network, here bit-shift decays and event caps. The constraints that come from the chip’s recurrent layout, the folded skips, hop delays, shared int8 scales, and integer thresholds, stay outside training and cost the bitshift-QAT backbone 31.1 31.1 top-1 points on Xylo Audio 3 (Table 6 ), which CAST recovers.

sections.heading: 6.4. Fine-Tuning the SEE with CAST
sections.text: The SEE’s 32 32 readout neurons follow the integer update of Eq. ( 26 ) with two differences: each emits at most one event per timestep, and its leak removes at least one unit from any positive state. We extend the CAST replica to the readout with these two rules, and its trainable parameters are again the chip’s int8 weights and integer thresholds. The readout replica reproduces all of XyloSim’s readout spikes. With the CAST backbone fixed, XyloSim produces its spikes once for every training window, and the SEE is fine-tuned on them through the readout replica with the episodic objective of its pretraining (Sec. 5.2 ). The readout thus learns the spikes the chip actually produces. The backbone and the SEE are written to the chip as one configuration of int8 weights, integer thresholds, and bit-shift decays, shared by every device.

sections.heading: 7. Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate HyVox as a few-shot open-set recognizer, to simulate the deployment-time situation in which a user enrolls new speakers from a single recording by forward passes alone, using audio that was never used to train HyVox . Sec. 7.1 defines the datasets, the few-shot protocol, the metrics, and the training budgets. Sec. 7.2 compares HyVox with the baselines on recognition and system cost. Sec. 7.3 isolates the contribution of each HTA design choice at the deployed neuron and synapse budget. Sec. 7.4 reports the HTA-SNN backbone on held-out VoxCeleb2. Sec. 7.5 isolates the contribution of each SEE design choice on the frozen backbone. Sec. 7.6 evaluates the full HyVox system, backbone and SEE, on few-shot recognition in simulated households. Sec. 7.7 describes the three training steps that deploy HyVox on Xylo Audio 3 and evaluates the deployed system on the chip.

sections.heading: 7.1. Evaluation Methodology
sections.text: Datasets. Each stage of HyVox uses a disjoint speaker population. The backbone is pretrained on VoxCeleb2 ( Chung et al., 2018 ) ( 2.05 2.05 M three-second segments, 5994 5994 speakers) and evaluated on a per-speaker stratified hold-out of 224,760 224{,}760 segments from the same speakers. The SEE is pretrained on VoxCeleb1 ( Nagrani et al., 2017 ) (Sec. 5.2 ), whose 1251 1251 speakers are absent from VoxCeleb2. Few-shot recognition is evaluated on Common Voice ( Ardila et al., 2020 ) , whose speakers are unseen by both the backbone and the SEE. All audio passes through a software model of the Xylo Audio 3 audio front end (AFE), giving a 16 16 -channel spike raster. The chip clips this raster to 15 15 events per bin, which enters only the deployment steps of Sec. 7.7 . Few-shot household protocol. We build 20 20 Common Voice speaker pools of 10 10 male and 10 10 female speakers who share one accent label, with no speaker in two pools. Pools are assigned round-robin over the accents, so they span 8 8 accents. Each pool yields one household of every size n ∈ { 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 , 14 , 18 , 20 } n\in\{2,4,6,8,10,14,18,20\} from its first n / 2 n/2 male and n / 2 n/2 female speakers, so sizes are nested and gender balanced. Each member is enrolled from their first 60 ​ s 60\,\mathrm{s} ( 29 29 windows at a 2 ​ s 2\,\mathrm{s} stride; Sec. 5.3 ). The next 120 ​ s 120\,\mathrm{s} yield 40 40 non-overlapping query windows. Each decision averages the latest W = 3 W=3 windows in a sliding fashion, so after the first 9 ​ s 9\,\mathrm{s} a new decision is issued every 3 ​ s 3\,\mathrm{s} , giving 38 38 decisions per speaker. Following openFEAT ( C et al., 2022 ) , 50 ​ n 50n guest decisions are drawn uniformly at random from speakers outside the household, regardless of accent, so about 10 % 10\% of guest decisions come from speakers who share the household’s accent. Metrics. All scores are cosine similarities of L2-normalized embeddings, mean-centred for the SEE (Sec. 5.1 ). On households, top-1 is the fraction of member decisions assigned to the correct prototype, and rejection EER is the operating point of the rejection threshold on s max s_{\max} , the highest cosine similarity between a decision and any enrolled prototype (Sec. 5.3 ), at which the fraction of guests accepted equals the fraction of members rejected; both are averaged over households. For the backbone, top-1 assigns each held-out VoxCeleb2 segment to the nearest of the 5994 5994 normalized AAM-Softmax class vectors (no margin), measuring separation of the training identities, and EER over 50,000 50{,}000 random pairs of VoxCeleb1 windows ( 20 20 per speaker) measures transfer to unseen speakers, the condition under which the SEE uses the backbone. Ablation protocol. We run two ablation studies, one on the HTA-SNN backbone (temporal stages, skip connections, and synaptic timescales) and one on the SEE (training objective, centring, and readout weights). Each study changes one design factor at a time and keeps all others fixed. Δ \Delta is each variant’s difference from its reference, reported with a 95% confidence interval (Secs. 7.3 and 7.5 ). The HTA-SNN ablations vary the backbone, and their reference is the deployed HTA-SNN. Every backbone variant has 832 832 LIF neurons and exactly 30,024 30{,}024 synapses ( 29,000 29{,}000 pruned weights plus the unpruned 1024 1024 -weight input projection, within the 31,744 31{,}744 -synapse budget). Every backbone variant is trained with the full pipeline and epoch budget of the deployed backbone (Sec. 7.4 ): 1000 1000 epochs of AAM-Softmax pretraining, the same SpikeFit pruning schedule ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) , and 30 30 epochs of bitshift QAT. Table 2 gives each variant’s best pretraining and pruning learning rates, and bitshift QAT uses 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} for every variant. The SEE ablations vary the SEE on the same frozen HTA-SNN backbone, and their reference is the mean-centred SEE (Sec. 5.1 ). Every SEE variant keeps the 32 32 -neuron int8 readout and is evaluated on the 151 151 VoxCeleb1 test speakers, and every trained SEE variant follows the pretraining recipe of the SEE (Secs. 5.2 and 7.5 ). Baselines. On households we compare against four reproduced ANN baselines: the small-footprint verification network of Balian et al. ( Balian et al., 2021 ) (Small-footprint SV), DS-CNN-S ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , BC-ResNet-1 ( Kim et al., 2021 ) , and MLP-d128, a dense framewise control with HTA-SNN’s input and hidden width. Each is pretrained on VoxCeleb2 with AAM-Softmax on its native-width embedding and enrolled and scored like HyVox . DS-CNN-S and BC-ResNet-1, keyword-spotting classifiers, take a linear embedding layer at their pooled width ( 64 64 and 20 20 ) for this pretraining. SynNet ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; Bos and Muir, 2024 ) , the reference SNN for Xylo, is the spiking baseline for the backbone (Sec. 7.4 ). It tiles a fixed bank of eight timescales ( 2 2 – 256 256 ) across each layer, has no skip connections, and is trained with the full pipeline of the deployed backbone at the same neuron and synapse budget. System metrics. ANN baselines run as int8 models on an STM32U575ZIT6Q ( STMicroelectronics, 2024b ) ( 2 ​ MB 2\,\mathrm{MB} flash, 786 ​ KB 786\,\mathrm{KB} SRAM) and HTA-SNN on Xylo Audio 3, both at 50 ​ MHz 50\,\mathrm{MHz} . Execution time covers loading the window’s input into the device and the forward pass. sections.text: The ablations identify which design factors of the HTA-SNN backbone (Sec. 4 ) account for its accuracy: the temporal stages, the skip connections, and the learned timescales and their initialization. Each ablation changes one factor, keeps all others fixed, and holds the deployed neuron and synapse budget (Sec. 7.1 ). Table 2 groups the variants by factor below HTA-SNN. At the shared learning rates, training collapses with linear-uniform initialization, and pruning collapses without skip A. For these variants and the variant without both skips, a learning-rate sweep selects the rates listed in Table 2 . All three skip variants share the highest pruning rate that is stable without skip A, which keeps the skip rows comparable. Δ \Delta is each variant’s difference from HTA-SNN. To quantify evaluation uncertainty, we resample the test speakers with replacement 1,000 1{,}000 times and score HTA-SNN and every variant on each resample. The 95% confidence interval is [ Δ 2.5 , Δ 97.5 ] [\Delta_{2.5},\,\Delta_{97.5}] , the 2.5 2.5 th and 97.5 97.5 th percentiles of the 1,000 1{,}000 resampled Δ \Delta . Resampling whole speakers keeps the correlated segments of each speaker together. Temporal stages. The stage variants remove one temporal stage at a time and reassign its neurons to the adjacent stages (local to medium; medium split between local and global; global to medium), reattaching both skip connections to the nearest remaining stage. The neuron count is therefore unchanged, and the widths in parentheses give the resulting local, medium, and global stage sizes. Every removal degrades both metrics. The global stage is the most important ( − 3.4 -3.4 top-1, + 1.3 +1.3 EER). Since its neurons remain in the network, this loss is attributable to the long integration window itself. Removing the local stage costs 2.0 2.0 top-1 and 0.8 0.8 EER points, and removing the medium stage costs 0.6 0.6 top-1 and 0.6 0.6 EER points. Skip connections. The skip variants remove skip A (input projection to global stage), skip B (local stage to readout), or both. Each skip benefits identification: removing skip A costs 3.4 3.4 top-1 points, removing skip B 4.7 4.7 , and removing both 6.2 6.2 . Skip A also benefits transfer to unseen speakers, with EER 0.9 0.9 points higher without it; the EER change of the other two variants ( + 0.1 +0.1 ) lies within its 95% confidence interval and thus remains comparable with HTA-SNN. Learned versus fixed timescales. The timescale variants replace the learned per-neuron τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} of HTA-SNN with a single fixed value shared by all four trainable stages. No fixed value matches the learned timescales on unseen speakers: every setting raises EER by 1.8 1.8 – 3.6 3.6 points. Fixed timescales also force a trade-off between the two metrics. The shortest timescale ( τ syn = 2 \tau_{\mathrm{syn}}=2 ) improves top-1 on the training identities by 0.8 0.8 points, yet raises EER by 2.1 2.1 points, which indicates overfitting to the pretraining speakers. Longer timescales degrade both metrics: τ syn = 4 \tau_{\mathrm{syn}}=4 costs 1.4 1.4 top-1 and 1.8 1.8 EER points, and τ syn = 16 \tau_{\mathrm{syn}}=16 costs 12.2 12.2 top-1 and 3.6 3.6 EER points. sections.heading: 7.5. SEE Ablation Studies
sections.text: The SEE ablations identify which design factors of the SEE (Sec. 5 ) account for its accuracy: the training objective, the centring, and the way the readout weights are obtained. Every variant is trained and evaluated on top of the same frozen HTA-SNN backbone (Sec. 4.2.1 ), so only the SEE and its training change. Each ablation changes one factor and keeps all others fixed, including the 32 32 -neuron int8 readout and the centring of every embedding unless centring is the factor. Every trained variant follows the pretraining recipe of the SEE (Sec. 5.2 ), and every checkpoint is selected on the VoxCeleb1 validation speakers. Table 4 reports top-1 identification and open-set EER on the 151 151 VoxCeleb1 test speakers, which no variant sees during training or selection, over 500 500 episodes in the pretraining format (Sec. 5.2 ). Each episode enrolls 20 20 speakers from 4 4 windows each, identifies 5 5 further windows per enrolled speaker, and rejects 5 5 windows from each of 5 5 unenrolled speakers. Δ \Delta is each variant’s difference from the SEE. To quantify evaluation uncertainty, we resample the 500 500 test episodes with replacement 1,000 1{,}000 times and score the SEE and every variant on each resample. The 95% confidence interval is [ Δ 2.5 , Δ 97.5 ] [\Delta_{2.5},\,\Delta_{97.5}] , the 2.5 2.5 th and 97.5 97.5 th percentiles of the 1,000 1{,}000 resampled Δ \Delta . Resampling whole episodes keeps the enrolled and unenrolled speakers of each episode together. Training objective. The objective variants remove the rejection loss ( λ = 0 \lambda=0 ) or replace the episodic objective with closed-set AAM-Softmax over the 900 900 training speakers, whose class weights are discarded after training. Removing ℒ rej \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rej}} costs 2.2 2.2 top-1 and 1.8 1.8 EER points. Closed-set training costs 5.7 5.7 top-1 and 6.0 6.0 EER points, the largest EER loss among the trained variants. A readout trained to separate a fixed set of speakers therefore transfers poorly to speakers enrolled from a few windows. Centring. The centring variant scores the normalised spike count 𝐫 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{r}} directly, with 𝝁 = 𝟎 \boldsymbol{\mu}=\mathbf{0} in training and inference. Without centring, top-1 drops by 3.9 3.9 points and EER rises by 2.3 2.3 points. Removing the component that all non-negative spike-count embeddings share improves both identification and rejection. Readout weights. The readout variants keep the readout and the centring and change how the readout’s 32 × 128 32\times 128 projection matrix 𝐖 s \mathbf{W}_{s} (Sec. 5.1 ), which maps the backbone’s 128 128 output spikes to the 32 32 readout neurons, is obtained. An untrained readout at its random initialization costs 20.7 20.7 top-1 and 7.5 7.5 EER points. The principal component analysis (PCA) ( Pearson, 1901 ) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) ( Fisher, 1936 ; Dehak et al., 2011 ) variants set 𝐖 s \mathbf{W}_{s} in closed form, with no episodic training. Each computes 32 32 projection directions from the backbone’s mean spike rates over the windows of the 900 900 training speakers and loads them as the rows of 𝐖 s \mathbf{W}_{s} in the same int8 readout, scaled by one input gain chosen on the VoxCeleb1 validation speakers. PCA keeps the directions of largest variance without using speaker labels, and LDA keeps the directions that maximise the ratio of between-speaker to within-speaker variance. Both recover part of the loss of the untrained readout. PCA costs 8.6 8.6 top-1 and 3.3 3.3 EER points, and LDA costs 7.1 7.1 top-1 and 1.3 1.3 EER points. Initializing 𝐖 s \mathbf{W}_{s} from PCA before episodic training costs 5.6 5.6 top-1 and 5.1 5.1 EER points, so the episodic objective reaches a better readout from a random start. Table 4 . sections.heading: 7.6. Few-Shot Speaker Recognition with HyVox
sections.text: HyVox combines the deployed HTA-SNN backbone (Sec. 7.4 ) with the SEE pretrained on VoxCeleb1 (Sec. 5.2 ). The members of each household are enrolled by forward passes of their enrollment speech through HyVox , which yield one prototype per member (Sec. 5.4 ), under the protocol of Sec. 7.1 . We report identification as the household grows, rejection of unseen speakers, and the embedding geometry behind both. Household scaling. Fig. 8 a shows top-1 identification over all eight household sizes; we report the mean over the 20 20 households with its 95% confidence interval. Top-1 falls from 99.6 ± 0.6 % 99.6\pm 0.6\% at n = 2 n=2 to 94.9 ± 1.2 % 94.9\pm 1.2\% at n = 20 n=20 . The decline flattens as the household grows: the six members added from n = 2 n=2 to n = 8 n=8 lower top-1 by 3.0 3.0 points, to 96.6 ± 1.2 % 96.6\pm 1.2\% , and the twelve added from n = 8 n=8 to n = 20 n=20 lower it by a further 1.7 1.7 points. The interval stays within ± 1.3 \pm 1.3 points at every size. Figure 8 . Household identification and unseen-speaker rejection by HyVox . (a) Top-1 identification; (b) rejection EER; (c) detection error tradeoff; (d) FAR (solid) and FRR (dashed) against ϑ rej \vartheta_{\mathrm{rej}} . Error bars, crosses, and bands are 95% confidence intervals over 20 20 households; dots mark the EER. Unseen-speaker rejection. Fig. 8 b – d evaluate the open-set decision against guests. Rejection EER rises from 5.5 ± 1.8 % 5.5\pm 1.8\% at n = 2 n=2 to 13.2 ± 0.9 % 13.2\pm 0.9\% at n = 20 n=20 (Fig. 8 b , mean and 95% confidence interval over households). A member is identified correctly as long as the correct prototype outscores the other n − 1 n-1 . A guest is rejected only if its similarity to every one of the n n prototypes stays below the threshold. The guest score s max s_{\max} is a maximum over n n cosines and grows with n n . Because the operating threshold depends on the application ( Tan et al., 2021 ) , Fig. 8 c plots the detection error tradeoff over all thresholds, which gives the false reject rate (FRR) at any false accept rate (FAR). At every FAR, FRR increases with n n , so a larger household raises the error at every operating point. Fig. 8 d plots both error rates against the threshold ϑ rej \vartheta_{\mathrm{rej}} . The EER threshold moves from 0.78 0.78 at n = 2 n=2 to 0.83 0.83 at n = 20 n=20 , and the FAR curve steepens and shifts right as n n grows. A threshold fixed at the n = 2 n=2 EER point therefore admits 32.1 % 32.1\% of guests at n = 20 n=20 , while rejecting 5.8 % 5.8\% of members, so the host sets ϑ rej \vartheta_{\mathrm{rej}} according to the number of enrolled speakers. Embedding geometry. Fig. 9 projects the HyVox embeddings of one household (United States English) with a single t-SNE ( van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008 ) fitted over all points; the three panels differ only in how many speakers are enrolled, and the guest sample is identical across them. At n = 2 n=2 the two prototypes lie at the edges of the guest cloud. At n = 20 n=20 the prototypes cover much of the region the guests occupy, so a guest decision lies nearer its closest prototype. This is the growth of the guest s max s_{\max} that raises the EER threshold in Fig. 8 d . The projection is qualitative, and the quantitative distances are those reported in Fig. 8 b – d . sections.heading: 7.7. On-Device Evaluation
sections.text: Figure 10 . Deploying the HTA-SNN backbone on Xylo Audio 3. (A) Synapse compression; hatched bars: VoxCeleb2 top-1. (B) Synapses kept per component. (C) Bitshift QAT and (D) CAST fine-tuning on held-out VoxCeleb1 speakers; dotted lines: the model from the previous step. HyVox runs on Xylo Audio 3 chip with an STM32L476 host. Fitting the network to the chip takes three training steps after pretraining: synapse compression to the chip’s weight budget, quantization-aware training (QAT) of the weights and timescales for the chip’s integer dynamics, and CAST fine-tuning under the chip’s event limits. Fig. 10 reports the three steps, and Fig. 11 the household evaluation of the deployed system. Every step trains on VoxCeleb2; we measure each step on held-out VoxCeleb1 speakers, who are unseen in training, and report VoxCeleb2 only for the synapse-compression schedule. Synapse compression. The dense backbone has 188.4 188.4 k prunable synapses, 5.9 × 5.9\times the 31.7 31.7 k budget of the chip’s recurrent weight matrix. We prune it with SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) in 14 14 steps over 1,255 1{,}255 epochs of compression-aware fine-tuning, which leaves 29.0 29.0 k synapses ( 15.4 % 15.4\% , 6.5 × 6.5\times compression) (Fig. 10 A ). After the QAT below, the compressed backbone reaches 39.6 % 39.6\% top-1 on held-out VoxCeleb2, against 50.7 % 50.7\% for the dense backbone. Pruning is global i.e. each step keeps the top-scoring synapses across all stages and skips together, with no per-layer quota, so the kept share differs by component (Fig. 10 B ): skip A ( 27.6 % 27.6\% ) and the local stage ( 26.9 % 26.9\% ) keep nearly twice the overall rate, the global stage keeps 18.7 % 18.7\% , and the readout, medium stage, and skip B keep 11.6 % 11.6\% or less. QAT of weights and timescales. The chip stores weights as integers and realizes every synaptic decay as a bit shift. Compression fine-tuning trains the weights against their quantization codebooks (Sec. 6.1 ), and before the last pruning step every τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} is snapped to the power-of-two grid and frozen. Bitshift QAT then replaces the floating-point LIF update with the chip’s integer bitshift update and trains the network for 30 30 epochs on VoxCeleb2. Fig. 10 C tracks the 20-way top-1 (Sec. 5.2 ) and open-set EER of the backbone embedding on held-out VoxCeleb1 validation speakers. On the 151 151 VoxCeleb1 test speakers, used neither for training nor for checkpoint selection (Table 5 ), integer dynamics without QAT cost 37.2 37.2 top-1 and 9.3 9.3 EER points against the unquantized model, and the QAT model ends 1.2 1.2 top-1 points above it and 1.0 1.0 EER point below. CAST fine-tuning. Fig. 10 D tracks CAST fine-tuning (Sec. 6.3 ) on the VoxCeleb1 validation speakers, where it recovers most of the loss of mapping the QAT backbone directly to the chip. On the test speakers (Table 5 ), the directly mapped backbone loses 29.9 29.9 top-1 and 6.4 6.4 EER points against the unquantized model, and after CAST it differs from it by 0.4 0.4 and 0.1 0.1 points, both within their 95% confidence intervals. The SEE is then fine-tuned on the chip’s backbone spikes (Sec. 6.4 ), with the centring vector 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} re-estimated from the chip’s readout counts. On the CAST backbone, the pretrained SEE without this fine-tuning reaches 42.3 % 42.3\% top-1 and 43.1 % 43.1\% EER on the VoxCeleb1 validation speakers; fine-tuning raises top-1 to 58.5 % 58.5\% and lowers the EER to 36.0 % 36.0\% . These VoxCeleb1 errors are far higher than the household errors of Sec. 7.6 because the VoxCeleb1 episodes are a much harder protocol. Each episode enrolls 20 20 speakers from only 4 4 windows each and scores every 3 ​ s 3\,\mathrm{s} query window on its own, and the windows come from in-the-wild interviews whose channel and background noise vary within a speaker. A household member is enrolled from 29 29 windows of read Common Voice speech, and each decision averages W = 3 W=3 windows. The hardness of the VoxCeleb1 episodes, used both to train and to evaluate the SEE, is deliberate. It keeps accuracy far from saturation, so the cost of each chip constraint and the gain of each training step remain measurable. The Common Voice households relax these conditions to those of a practical deployment and measure the accuracy of the deployed system. Table 5 . Mapped directly, the bitshift-QAT model loses 31.1 31.1 top-1 points and gains 7.4 7.4 EER points against its own PyTorch accuracy on the test speakers. To locate this loss, we replicate the chip’s neuron update in PyTorch with each chip constraint switchable. With every constraint off, the replica matches the PyTorch model, and with every constraint on, it matches Xylo Audio 3. We then add the constraints to the trained model one at a time (Table 6 ). Four constraints each cost 18 18 to 32 32 top-1 points on their own. The chip caps every neuron at 31 31 output events per time step. It stores weights as 8-bit integers (int8) with one scale per destination layer, so a few large weights set the scale and round many small weights to zero, and the skip paths, folded into the same recurrent matrix, share that scale. Every hidden-to-hidden connection adds a one-step delay. Finally, the trained floating-point thresholds are mapped to the chip’s integer thresholds. We retrained the whole pipeline from random initialization with them. In PyTorch this model reaches 59.1 % 59.1\% top-1, and on the chip it falls to 30.0 % 30.0\% , no better than the directly mapped QAT model, because the int8 grid, the threshold mapping, and the hop delays remain. With per-neuron int8 scales and its trained thresholds, it still reaches only 46.8 % 46.8\% top-1 on the chip. Training with the caps thus recovers little of the chip’s loss, so the network has to be trained through all four constraints together. CAST trains through all of these constraints together. After 26 26 epochs it comes within 1.6 1.6 top-1 and 1.1 1.1 EER points of the PyTorch model on the chip, confirming on the test speakers the validation result of Fig. 10 D , and it exceeds the model trained with caps by 30.7 30.7 top-1 and 8.3 8.3 EER points with the standard mapping and by 13.9 13.9 and 3.8 3.8 points with the per-neuron mapping. CAST trains one integer firing threshold per neuron, which acts as a per-neuron gain. Across neurons, the thresholds span 3 3 to 16 16 in the directly mapped model and 1 1 to 142 142 after CAST. Strongly driven neurons receive high thresholds and fire below the 31 31 -event cap, and weakly driven neurons receive low ones, so the share of active steps at the cap falls from 98.5 % 98.5\% to 3.7 % 3.7\% and graded counts reach the readout. CAST is thus the step that makes the backbone deployable, recovering 29.5 29.5 of the 31.1 31.1 top-1 points that the chip’s constraints cost. Hardware deployment. The deployed network consists of the CAST HTA-SNN and the SEE, stored as int8 weights, integer thresholds, and power-of-two decay shifts. We place these parameters into the chip’s input, recurrent, and readout weight matrices, which gives the configuration that is written to Xylo Audio 3. The synapse counts in this paper, including the 29.0 29.0 k of the compressed backbone, refer to the trained network, where each skip connection is a separate projection layer. The chip has no skip layers, so each skip projection is multiplied into the layer it feeds and stored as direct recurrent synapses, which adds synapses on the skip paths, while int8 rounding sets the smallest weights to zero. The chip configuration therefore holds 27,259 27{,}259 recurrent synapses, within its budget of 31,744 31{,}744 . One configuration serves every household, since HyVox holds no household-specific weight. Each 3 ​ s 3\,\mathrm{s} window enters the chip as its AFE spike raster, starts from a reset state, and returns the 32 32 readout spike counts, and the host forms prototypes and decisions as in Sec. 6.5 . We evaluate 20 20 households of 10 10 female and 10 10 male speakers in four accent groups, which share no speaker with the households of Sec. 7.6 , with the enrollment, query, guest, and sliding W = 3 W=3 decision protocol of Sec. 7.1 . As the reference, we evaluate the PyTorch model of Sec. 7.6 (Fig. 8 ), the bitshift-QAT backbone with the pretrained SEE and without the chip’s event caps, on these households. Fig. 11 shows that the deployed system on the chip matches or exceeds the PyTorch model. In Fig. 11 a and b , light bars give the PyTorch model and solid bars the on-device system, with 95% confidence intervals over the 20 20 households (reported as ± \pm ). Top-1 is 100.0 ± 0.0 % 100.0\pm 0.0\% , 98.6 ± 0.5 % 98.6\pm 0.5\% , and 96.7 ± 0.7 % 96.7\pm 0.7\% at n = 2 n=2 , 10 10 , and 20 20 (Fig. 11 a ), against 100.0 ± 0.0 % 100.0\pm 0.0\% , 97.8 ± 0.8 % 97.8\pm 0.8\% , and 95.3 ± 1.1 % 95.3\pm 1.1\% for the PyTorch model. The rejection EER is 3.8 ± 1.2 % 3.8\pm 1.2\% , 7.3 ± 0.9 % 7.3\pm 0.9\% , and 10.0 ± 0.7 % 10.0\pm 0.7\% (Fig. 11 b ), against 4.3 ± 1.2 % 4.3\pm 1.2\% , 9.8 ± 1.1 % 9.8\pm 1.1\% , and 12.4 ± 0.8 % 12.4\pm 0.8\% . Paired over the 20 20 households, the two systems agree within their 95% confidence intervals at n = 2 n=2 and in top-1 at n = 10 n=10 . At n = 20 n=20 the chip is 1.4 ± 0.8 1.4\pm 0.8 points higher in top-1, and its EER is 2.5 ± 1.1 2.5\pm 1.1 and 2.4 ± 0.7 2.4\pm 0.7 points lower at n = 10 n=10 and 20 20 . This gain comes from the backbone trained through CAST. Although the CAST backbone trails the PyTorch backbone on the VoxCeleb1 test speakers (Table 5 ), it leads on the Common Voice households, whose read speech and home recording conditions differ from the interview recordings of the VoxCeleb2 training data. sections.heading: 8. Related Work
sections.text: Low-power audio inference rests on mature microcontroller and neuromorphic baselines, which include compact and end-to-end benchmarks ( Warden, 2018 ; Yik et al., 2025 ) , efficient keyword-spotting backbones ( Zhang et al., 2017 ; Kim et al., 2021 ) , deployment toolchains ( David et al., 2021 ; Banbury et al., 2021 ; STMicroelectronics, 2022 ) , and on-device speaker identification ( Balian et al., 2021 ; Gallacher et al., 2023 ) . Neuromorphic processors run such workloads with sparse, event-driven computation ( Akopyan et al., 2015 ; Davies et al., 2018 ; Furber et al., 2014 ; Moradi et al., 2018 ; Davies et al., 2021 ) . Two such chips have been applied to audio. Intel’s Loihi is a research chip with many neuromorphic cores and on-chip learning ( Davies et al., 2018 ; Davies et al., 2021 ) , and keyword spotting and signal processing on it use far less energy per inference than on conventional processors ( Blouw et al., 2019 ; Blouw and Eliasmith, 2020 ) . SynSense’s Xylo is a family of low-power inference chips for edge sensing, and Xylo Audio 3 pairs an analog audio front-end with a digital core of 1,000 1{,}000 spiking neurons ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; SynSense, 2023 ) , running audio applications at sub-milliwatt power ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; Bos and Muir, 2024 ) . These systems have traditionally been built to recognize a set of labels fixed at training time, so adding a class means collecting its data and retraining the network. Modern-day speaker recognition systems have moved from GMMs and i-vectors to neural embeddings ( Reynolds et al., 2000 ; Dehak et al., 2011 ; Variani et al., 2014 ; Snyder et al., 2018 ) , and strong encoders ( Okabe et al., 2018 ; Desplanques et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) are trained on large datasets with over 7,000 7{,}000 speakers and over a million utterances ( Nagrani et al., 2017 ; Chung et al., 2018 ) , using metric objectives such as GE2E, angular margins, and supervised contrastive learning ( Wan et al., 2018 ; Deng et al., 2019 ; Khosla et al., 2020 ) . An encoder maps each utterance to a fixed-length embedding, and speakers are compared by the cosine similarity of their embeddings, so a new speaker can be enrolled from a recording without retraining. Few-shot learning builds a class representation from a handful of examples, often as the mean embedding of the class ( Snell et al., 2017 ) , and open-set recognition rejects inputs from classes that were absent at training time ( Scheirer et al., 2013 ; Geng et al., 2021 ; Vaze et al., 2022 ) . Few-shot open-set learning combines the two and trains on episodes that each enroll new classes and reject unknown ones ( Liu et al., 2020 ) , and openFEAT applies it to speaker identification in households that share a device ( C et al., 2022 ; Tan et al., 2021 ) . Spiking neurons integrate their input over time in a membrane state and communicate through binary events, which suits sparse, low-power hardware. LIF dynamics ( Gerstner and Kistler, 2002 ) and surrogate gradients ( Neftci et al., 2019 ; Zenke and Ganguli, 2018 ; Bellec et al., 2018 ; Shrestha and Orchard, 2018 ; Wu et al., 2018 ) make deep SNNs trainable, and residual, hybrid, and transformer designs ( Lee et al., 2020 ; Rathi et al., 2020 ; Fang et al., 2021 ; Deng et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) scale them to larger tasks, beyond the neuron and synapse budget of a neuromorphic chip. Large sparse networks outperform small dense ones of the same size ( Zhu and Gupta, 2017 ) , SpikeFit prunes SNN channels for neuromorphic deployment and was evaluated on an image classifier that runs for four timesteps ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) , and quantization-aware training adapts networks to integer arithmetic ( Jacob et al., 2018 ; Bengio et al., 2013 ) . Hardware-in-the-loop training runs the forward pass on an analog chip such as BrainScaleS-2 and computes gradients through a software model of it ( Schmitt et al., 2017 ; Cramer et al., 2022 ) . The toolchains of digital chips, such as Rockpool for Xylo ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ) , model the chip’s bit-shift decays and per-step event caps during training.

sections.heading: 9. Discussion and Future Work
sections.text: HyVox targets personalized speaker identification on always-on devices with a small local gallery, such as shared smart speakers, hearables, and home appliances that tailor their responses to each enrolled user. The neuromorphic chip computes the embedding of every window, and the microcontroller keeps the gallery local and mutable, so users are enrolled and rejected without any change to the network on the chip. Two properties bound this operating point. Rejection becomes harder as the gallery grows, since a guest is compared against every enrolled prototype, and the rejection EER rises from 5.5 % 5.5\% with two members to 13.2 % 13.2\% with twenty (Sec. 7.6 ). HyVox therefore suits applications in which a wrong decision changes a response, and a security-critical application would need a lower error rate or a second factor. The chip’s 32 32 readout neurons are also the only interface between the two processors, so they bound the dimension of the embedding. Because the gallery lives on the host, it can follow its users over long deployments. The host can decide when a new enrollment is distinct enough to accept, refresh a prototype as a user’s voice changes with age, and recalibrate the threshold table of Sec. 6.5 as the gallery grows, all without retraining the network. Our future work follows two directions. The first is to follow households over years. A speaker’s voice changes as they age, and each speaker in our households contributes a few minutes of speech, so change over years has not been considered. We plan to collect recordings of the same households over multiple years and use them to design host policies that refresh a member’s prototype from confidently identified decisions and recalibrate the rejection threshold as the household changes, without retraining the network. The second direction is hardware–algorithm co-design for future neuromorphic chips. CAST measures the accuracy cost of each hardware constraint separately (Table 6 ), which makes it a tool for chip design as well as a training method. Before a chip is built, its design simulator can serve as the bit-exact model of its update, and CAST can train a network through each candidate set of event limits, weight formats, state widths, and readout widths. We plan to choose the constraints of future chips by weighing the accuracy each candidate reaches against its silicon area and power, and to understand when training through hardware constraints improves generalization, so that the limits of a chip can be designed to strengthen its models as well as to save energy.

sections.heading: 10. Conclusion
sections.text: We presented HyVox , a hybrid neuromorphic–von Neumann system for open-set speaker identification on always-on devices, pairing a spiking embedding processor on Xylo Audio 3 with a lightweight host for prototype scoring, enrollment, and rejection. On 20 20 Common Voice households of unseen speakers, HyVox reached 99.6 % 99.6\% top-1 accuracy and 5.5 % 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 2 members and 94.9 % 94.9\% and 13.2 % 13.2\% with 20 20 . On 20 20 further households, the deployed chip matched or exceeded the PyTorch model it was fine-tuned from. Each three-second window cost 0.96 ​ s 0.96\,\mathrm{s} and 1.63 ​ mJ 1.63\,\mathrm{mJ} of dynamic energy, with 42 % 42\% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5 × 13.5\times less dynamic and 5.8 × 5.8\times less total energy than the most energy-efficient one. These results show that neuromorphic audio hardware can serve as the low-power embedding substrate for open-set speaker recognition at the edge.
