In this paper, we present HyVox , a hybrid neuromorphic–von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification under extremely tight energy budgets . HyVox splits the workload at the speaker embedding. A neuromorphic processor embeds the speech with sparse, event-driven computation, and a von Neumann microcontroller holds the speaker gallery and makes every decision: it scores queries by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing a prototype, with no weight update. On the neuromorphic processor, a hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone learns a synaptic time constant per leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, allocating 832 832 neurons across fast, medium, and slow timescales. A 32 32 -neuron spiking embedding extractor (SEE), pretrained on episodes that each enroll new speakers and reject outsiders, turns the backbone output into an embedding for speakers unseen in training; its 32 32 spike counts are the only interface between the two processors. To fit the chip’s synapse and integer budgets, we compress the backbone 6.5 × 6.5\times to 29.0 29.0 k synapses, train it for integer bit-shift dynamics, and fine-tune it with chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). CAST trains through a differentiable replica of the chip’s integer neuron update, derived from its cycle-accurate simulator, so that gradient descent optimizes the exact weights and thresholds the chip runs; it doubles the top-1 accuracy of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers. On 20 20 Common Voice households of unseen speakers, HyVox reaches 99.6 % 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5 % 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 2 members and 94.9 % 94.9\% and 13.2 % 13.2\% with 20 20 , and the network deployed on the neuromorphic chip matches its trained model. Each inference on a 3 3 -s window takes 0.96 ​ s 0.96\,\mathrm{s} and 1.63 ​ mJ 1.63\,\mathrm{mJ} of dynamic energy, 42 % 42\% lower latency than the fastest embedded ANN baseline and 13.5 × 13.5\times less dynamic and 5.8 × 5.8\times less total energy than the most energy-efficient one. 1. Introduction Motivation. Smart audio devices are moving from fixed command recognition ( Warden, 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; Kim et al., 2021 ) toward personalized speaker identity ( Variani et al., 2014 ; Snyder et al., 2018 ; Gallacher et al., 2023 ) . A shared smart speaker adds household members after it is installed, a hearable recognizes its owner, and a home appliance tailors its responses to the enrolled user who speaks and treats strangers as guests. In each case the speakers that matter are defined after deployment ( Snell et al., 2017 ; Wan et al., 2018 ) : the device enrolls a new user from a short recording, keeps that user’s representation in local memory, compares every query against a gallery that changes over time, and rejects speech from anyone who is not enrolled ( Scheirer et al., 2013 ; Geng et al., 2021 ; Vaze et al., 2022 ) . These operations run on battery-powered hardware, so the energy of the inference that turns a window of speech into speaker evidence bounds how many decisions the device can make on one charge ( David et al., 2021 ; Banbury et al., 2021 ; Yik et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1 . HyVox ’s concept: Hybrid platform for low-energy speaker identification Current Approaches and Limitations. Speaker identification on edge devices runs as a TinyML pipeline on a von Neumann microcontroller. A compact artificial neural network (ANN), such as DS-CNN ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , BC-ResNet ( Kim et al., 2021 ) , or the small-footprint speaker network of Balian et al. ( Balian et al., 2021 ) , embeds each window of audio, and the same microcontroller scores the embedding against a gallery of enrolled prototypes, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users. Scoring takes only a few dot products per enrolled speaker, so ANN inference accounts for nearly all of the energy of a decision. On a von Neumann core, each multiply–accumulate of this inference fetches its weight and activation from memory, so this data movement sets the energy of every inference. Neuromorphic processors such as Xylo Audio 3 ( SynSense, 2023 ) remove this traffic: an event-driven front end and spiking cores keep weights beside the neurons and compute only when spikes arrive. A neuromorphic core running a spiking neural network (SNN) is therefore a natural replacement for the ANN in the TinyML pipeline. Moving the entire open-set pipeline onto the neuromorphic core, however, is infeasible. The core executes only the SNN mapped onto it and has no general-purpose compute, so it cannot store a gallery that changes at runtime, normalize and compare embeddings, apply a rejection threshold, or enroll a speaker without reconfiguring the network. Existing neuromorphic audio work ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; Bos and Muir, 2024 ) accordingly targets closed-set classification and keyword spotting. The same co-location that saves energy also caps the network size: every weight occupies on-chip memory beside its neuron, so Xylo Audio 3 holds at most 1,000 1{,}000 spiking neurons and 31,744 31{,}744 int8 recurrent synapses, orders of magnitude below the millions of parameters of standard speaker encoders ( Snyder et al., 2018 ) . Two questions remain open: how to learn a speaker embedding that generalizes to unseen speakers within this fixed hardware budget, and how to design a system that combines the low-energy inference of a neuromorphic chip with the general-purpose compute that open-set recognition requires. Proposed Approach. In this paper, we present HyVox , a hybrid neuromorphic–von Neumann system for low-energy open-set speaker identification (Fig. 1 ). The central idea is to split the workload at the embedding: the neuromorphic core takes over the ANN’s role in the TinyML pipeline, and the von Neumann microcontroller (MCU) keeps every operation that needs general-purpose compute. Xylo Audio 3 runs the audio front end (AFE) and a spiking embedding network and emits one 32-component spike-count vector per inference on a three-second window. An STM32L476 MCU host turns these counts into decisions: it holds a gallery of speaker prototypes, scores each query by cosine similarity, rejects unknown speakers, and enrolls new users by writing a prototype. The spiking network is shared by every device and never trained on a user’s audio; each household differs only in the gallery on its host. Challenges. Moving the embedding from an ANN on the MCU to an SNN on the neuromorphic core places the whole burden of recognition on a network of fixed size, integer dynamics, and a 32 32 -neuron output, and that output must still support every open-set decision the MCU makes. This raises four challenges, from the design of the network to its execution on the chip: • Speaker evidence in a small SNN. Speaker evidence spans milliseconds (formant transitions, plosive releases) to hundreds of milliseconds (pitch contour, speaking rate). ANN encoders cover this range with depth and width, but the chip holds 1,000 1{,}000 neurons. In a spiking network the only memory of the past is each neuron’s decay, so the timescales assigned to so few neurons determine which speaker evidence the network can represent at all. • A 32 32 -dimensional spiking embedding for unseen speakers. The chip’s hidden state never leaves the chip; the MCU receives only the spike count of each of the 32 32 readout neurons per window. These counts are the entire interface, so they must serve directly as the embedding: they must identify speakers absent from training, enroll a new speaker from one minute of speech with no weight update, and separate speakers who were never enrolled so the MCU can reject them. Large-corpus pretraining separates a fixed set of training speakers and never practises enrollment or rejection. • Fitting the hardware’s synapse and precision budget. On-chip memory bounds the number of synapses; Xylo Audio 3 holds at most 31,744 31{,}744 . A fully connected network of five layers of width w w has four connections between adjacent layers of w 2 w^{2} synapses each, so the budget allows w ≈ 31,744 / 4 ≈ 89 w\approx\sqrt{31{,}744/4}\approx 89 , about 445 445 neurons in total. That is under half of Xylo’s 1,000 1{,}000 and too few to cover the timescales of speaker evidence. A network with enough neurons exceeds the synapse budget several times over and must lose most of its synapses to fit, and the hardware further restricts weights to low-precision integers and decays to a discrete set, int8 weights and power-of-two bit shifts on Xylo. Each of these steps removes speaker information that training must recover. • The gap between the trained network and the chip. Even after compression and quantization, the chip computes differently from the model used in training. On the chip, a neuron can fire only a limited number of times per timestep, signals take extra timesteps to pass from one layer to the next, and neuron state is clipped when it exceeds the register range. Training ignores all three, so the network learns to rely on behavior the chip cannot reproduce, and a network that recognizes speakers well in training can lose much of its accuracy once it runs on the chip. Technical Contributions. HyVox addresses these challenges with four matching contributions: • HTA-SNN backbone. We design a hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA) SNN backbone of 832 832 leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons that learns a synaptic time constant per neuron, so training allocates the neuron budget across timescales, with cross-scale projections that carry fast acoustic evidence to the slow stages (Sec. 4 ). At the same synapse budget, it exceeds SynNet ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ; Bos and Muir, 2024 ) , the reference SNN for Xylo, by 4.1 4.1 top-1 points and 1.6 1.6 equal error rate (EER) points. • Spiking embedding extractor (SEE). We propose a 32 32 -neuron spiking readout pretrained episodically on speakers disjoint from the backbone’s: every episode enrolls new speakers from a few windows and rejects speakers who are not enrolled (Sec. 5 ). Its normalized spike counts are the trained embedding, so the STM32 host holds every speaker-specific quantity, the gallery, a sliding three-window buffer, and a threshold per gallery size, enrolls a user with forward passes and a prototype write, and decides in under 10 3 10^{3} operations with 64 64 bytes per speaker, one signed 16-bit value per embedding dimension (Sec. 6.5 ). • Dense-to-sparse compression. Since a large sparse network outperforms a small dense one with the same number of weights ( Zhu and Gupta, 2017 ) , we train the backbone dense, with 188.4 188.4 k synapses ( 5.9 × 5.9\times the budget), and compress it 6.5 × 6.5\times to 29.0 29.0 k synapses, 15.4 % 15.4\% of the dense network, on a 293 293 -timestep task. To achieve this, we extend SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) , whose Fisher spike contribution scores channels and was demonstrated on a 4 4 -timestep image classifier at a single pruning ratio, to a per-synapse score ranked globally across stages and skip connections, and prune iteratively in 14 14 steps while the learned time constants settle onto the chip’s bit-shift grid (Sec. 6.1 ). Training the compressed network for the chip’s integer bitshift dynamics then recovers its accuracy before quantization (Secs. 6.2 and 7.7 ). • Chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). We derive a trainable PyTorch replica of the chip’s integer neuron update from the chip’s cycle-accurate simulator and fine-tune the network through it, a method that applies to any digital neuromorphic chip with such a simulator. Our CAST replica for Xylo reproduces 99.8 % 99.8\% of the simulator’s hidden spike counts exactly. Its trainable parameters are the chip’s own int8 weights and integer thresholds, so gradient descent optimizes the configuration the chip runs, under its event limits and per-layer delay. CAST doubles the top-1 of the mapped backbone on unseen speakers, from 31 % 31\% to 61 % 61\% (Sec. 7.7 ). We evaluate HyVox on 20 20 accent-homogeneous Common Voice households of speakers unseen by both the backbone and the SEE. HyVox reaches 99.6 % 99.6\% top-1 and 5.5 % 5.5\% rejection EER with 2 2 members and 94.9 % 94.9\% and 13.2 % 13.2\% with 20 20 . On 20 20 further households, the deployed system on the chip matches or exceeds the PyTorch model it was fine-tuned from, with 96.7 % 96.7\% top-1 and 10.0 % 10.0\% EER at n = 20 n=20 . HyVox reduces the inference energy. Each inference on a three-second window takes 0.96 ​ s 0.96\,\mathrm{s} and 1.63 ​ mJ 1.63\,\mathrm{mJ} of dynamic energy, 13.5 × 13.5\times less dynamic and 5.8 × 5.8\times less total energy than the most energy-efficient embedded ANN baseline, with a 42 % 42\% lower latency than the fastest one. 2. Background This section covers speaker embeddings and how TinyML pipelines compute them on embedded devices, spiking neural networks (SNNs) and the neuromorphic processors that run them, and how a trained SNN is fitted to neuromorphic hardware. Speaker embeddings and the TinyML pipeline. Speaker recognition is commonly framed as an embedding problem: an encoder maps each utterance to a vector whose geometry places same-speaker examples close together and different-speaker examples far apart ( Variani et al., 2014 ; Snyder et al., 2018 ) . Angular-margin classification ( Deng et al., 2019 ) learns this geometry from a large set of labelled training speakers, and supervised contrastive learning ( Khosla et al., 2020 ) shapes it directly over pairs of examples. In open-set recognition the deployed speakers are not known at training time ( Geng et al., 2021 ; Vaze et al., 2022 ) : the device enrolls each user as a normalized prototype ( Snell et al., 2017 ) , scores a query against every prototype by cosine similarity, and rejects the query when its best score falls below a threshold. Few-shot open-set learning ( Liu et al., 2020 ; C et al., 2022 ) trains for this use. Each training episode samples a new set of speakers, builds their prototypes from a few examples, classifies further examples of them, and includes speakers outside the set that must be rejected, so the model practises enrollment and rejection on speakers that change in every episode. On an edge device, the whole pipeline runs on one microcontroller ( David et al., 2021 ; Banbury et al., 2021 ) . A compact artificial neural network, such as DS-CNN ( Zhang et al., 2017 ) , BC-ResNet ( Kim et al., 2021 ) , or the speaker network of Balian et al. ( Balian et al., 2021 ) , computes the embedding from frame-level features such as mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), and the same core stores the gallery, scores, and enrolls. Spiking neural networks and neuromorphic processors. Neuromorphic audio systems encode sound as sparse events and process them with a spiking neural network (SNN) of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons ( Gerstner and Kistler, 2002 ) . Each neuron’s synaptic current and membrane voltage decay with time constants τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} and τ mem \tau_{\mathrm{mem}} , and the neuron spikes when its voltage crosses a threshold. These decays are a feed-forward SNN’s only memory of past input, so they set how far back each neuron integrates acoustic evidence. Surrogate gradients carry training through the non-differentiable spike ( Neftci et al., 2019 ) . Neuromorphic processors ( Akopyan et al., 2015 ; Davies et al., 2018 ; Bos and Muir, 2023 ) store each weight beside its neuron and compute only when spikes arrive ( Roy et al., 2019 ) , so the silicon fixes the size and arithmetic of the network. In Xylo Audio 3 ( SynSense, 2023 ) , an audio front end converts the microphone signal into a 16 16 -channel spike raster for its spiking core. Its limits are typical of the class: at most 1,000 1{,}000 hidden neurons and 31,744 31{,}744 int8 recurrent synapses; integer thresholds and 16 16 -bit saturating state; power-of-two decays; at most 31 31 events per hidden neuron and one per readout neuron per timestep; 32 32 readout neurons as the only off-chip output; and one timestep of delay per hidden-to-hidden hop. Fitting a trained network to neuromorphic hardware. Deploying an SNN trained in floating point on a neuromorphic chip involves three steps: pruning, quantization-aware training, and mapping. Pruning removes synapses until the network meets the synapse budget; at a fixed number of weights, pruning a large dense network yields higher accuracy than training a small dense one ( Zhu and Gupta, 2017 ) , and SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) adapts compression-aware fine-tuning to SNNs, pruning the channels with the lowest Fisher spike contribution. Quantization-aware training (QAT) ( Jacob et al., 2018 ) simulates the chip’s integer weights and bit-shift decays in the forward pass and passes gradients through the rounding with the straight-through estimator ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) . Mapping converts the trained parameters into the chip configuration, and a cycle-accurate simulator, such as XyloSim in Rockpool ( Bos and Muir, 2023 ) , predicts the spikes the chip will produce. 3. System Overview HyVox splits open-set speaker identification at the embedding. A spiking network on Xylo Audio 3 embeds each three-second window of audio, and an STM32L476 host keeps every operation that needs general-purpose compute. Fig. 2 shows the two parts of the system: an offline pipeline that trains the spiking network and fits it to the chip (right), and the hybrid neuromorphic audio platform that runs it on the device (left). Our four contributions form the offline pipeline. The HTA-SNN backbone and the SEE define the network, and dense-to-sparse compression and CAST fit it to the chip. The neuromorphic–von Neumann platform then runs the network, with the open-set gallery on the host. Figure 2 . HyVox system overview: offline training and mapping (right) and the inference pipeline (left). 3.1. Model Training and Mapping HTA-SNN backbone. The backbone is a hierarchical temporal abstraction SNN of 832 832 LIF neurons that learns a synaptic time constant per neuron and carries fast acoustic evidence to its slow stages through cross-scale projections (Sec. 4 ). It is pretrained as a speaker classifier on VoxCeleb2 from the 16 16 -channel spike rasters of the chip’s audio front end (AFE), so the network learns from the same input it receives on the device. Dense-to-sparse compression. The backbone is trained dense with 188.4 188.4 k synapses, 5.9 × 5.9\times the chip’s budget. Our per-synapse extension of SpikeFit ( Kartashov et al., 2025 ) then prunes it iteratively to 29.0 29.0 k synapses with compression-aware fine-tuning (Sec. 6.1 ), and quantization-aware training replaces the floating-point LIF update with the chip’s int8 weights and bit-shift decays (Sec. 6.2 ). Chip-accurate spiking training (CAST). The quantized backbone still runs without the chip’s event caps and per-hop delay. CAST fine-tunes it through a PyTorch replica of the chip’s integer neuron update, derived from the cycle-accurate simulator XyloSim, whose trainable parameters are the chip’s own int8 weights and integer thresholds. Training therefore optimizes the exact configuration that is written to the chip (Sec. 6.3 ). Spiking embedding extractor (SEE). With the backbone frozen, the SEE, a 32 32 -neuron spiking readout, is pretrained episodically on VoxCeleb1, whose speakers are disjoint from the backbone’s VoxCeleb2 speakers. Each episode enrolls new speakers from a few windows, identifies further windows of them, and rejects speakers who are not enrolled, so the readout learns the operations the device later performs on its users (Sec. 5 ). The SEE is finally fine-tuned on the chip-exact spikes of the CAST backbone. The backbone and the SEE are mapped once to a single Xylo configuration that serves every device; no weight is ever trained on a user’s audio. 3.2. Hybrid Neuromorphic Audio Platform Neuromorphic core. A 16 ​ kHz 16\,\mathrm{kHz} microphone feeds the AFE of Xylo Audio 3, which converts the waveform into a 16 16 -channel spike raster. Each three-second window of this raster drives the mapped HTA-SNN and SEE from a reset state, and the chip emits the spike counts of the 32 32 SEE neurons. This count vector is the only output of the chip and the entire interface to the host. Hybrid manager. The firmware’s hybrid manager mediates the chip–host boundary. A cycle scheduler issues a read trigger at the end of each window, the readout transfers the 32 32 counts over UART, and a mode controller sets the host to enrollment or identification. One decision moves 70 70 bytes per three-second window, independent of the size of the network on the chip. von Neumann core. The STM32 runs the metric kernel and holds every speaker-specific quantity. It L2-normalizes each count vector into the trained embedding, averages the latest three windows, scores the result against every prototype in the gallery by cosine similarity, and accepts the best match only if its score reaches a rejection threshold chosen for the current gallery size. In enrollment mode, the host accumulates the normalized embeddings of a new speaker’s windows into one prototype and writes it to the gallery. Adding or deleting a speaker is a write to host memory with 64 64 bytes per speaker, and the network on the chip is unchanged, so each household differs from another only in the gallery on its host (Sec. 6.5 ). 4. Hierarchical Temporal Abstraction (HTA) Speaker identity includes multiple temporal scales: short-timescale acoustic events (plosive releases, formant transitions, fricative onsets) cue vocal-tract structure, while longer patterns (speaking rate, pitch contour, slowly varying resonance) give more stable evidence over hundreds of milliseconds. Modern encoders capture this range with deep, over-parameterised temporal models ( Snyder et al., 2018 ; Desplanques et al., 2020 ) , but current neuromorphic hardware, including Xylo Audio 3 ( SynSense, 2023 ) , caps the deployed network at 1,000 1{,}000 neurons, 31,744 31{,}744 recurrent synapses, and low-precision integer weights. Naively reducing conventional architectures to this regime strips precisely the temporal capacity needed for robust discrimination; the architectural problem is thus not just fewer neurons, but allocating the remaining state to the right timescales. To overcome this, we propose hierarchical temporal abstraction (HTA), a compact LIF hierarchy for speaker embeddings. Its layers learn distinct integration windows, allowing fast acoustic cues and slower speaker patterns to be represented in the same model. Cross-scale projections carry short-timescale evidence forward while deeper layers accumulate long-range speaker context. 4.1. HTA’s Concept Our key observation is that the temporal depth in a spiking network is not determined only by the number of layers, but also by the temporal filtering applied before each neuron integrates its input. Hence, we distinguish the two LIF timescales explicitly. The membrane time constant τ mem \tau_{\mathrm{mem}} controls how long a neuron retains voltage after receiving current; in our model it is fixed at 2 2 timesteps for every neuron. The synaptic time constant τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} controls the temporal content delivered to the membrane by filtering presynaptic spike trains. This is the trainable quantity in HTA. Small τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} values preserve sharp transients, while larger τ syn \tau_{\mathrm{syn}} values expose the neuron to evidence integrated over longer intervals ( Gerstner and Kistler, 2002 ) . Proposed Backbone Our proposed HTA backbone receives a spike raster 𝐱 ∈ { 0 , 1 } T × 16 \mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{T\times 16} , where the 16 channels are produced by the Xylo Audio 3 audio front end (AFE) and T = 293 T=293 timesteps correspond to a 3-second utterance segment. Cross-Scale Fusion A strictly feed-forward temporal hierarchy creates a failure mode i.e. fast phonetic evidence must pass through progressively slower layers before it can affect the embedding. By the time it reaches the readout, transient structure may have been attenuated by repeated integration. HTA mitigates this bottleneck with two projected skip connections. The first injects the input projection 𝐡 1 \mathbf{h}_{1} into the long-range integrator, giving the global layer access to unsmoothed spectral evidence. The second injects the local representation 𝐡 2 \mathbf{h}_{2} into the readout integrator, preserving short-timescale articulatory cues alongside deeper context vector. These skips are not residual blocks in the conventional deep-network sense, they connect different channel widths and different temporal regimes. Their role is cross-scale fusion under a fixed neuron budget. The final embedding therefore reflects three complementary sources of information i.e. fast local events from early layers, intermediate acoustic trajectories, and long-range speaker context from the deeper integrators. 4.2.3. Spiking Embedding Extractor (SEE) Pretrained on VoxCeleb2 (Sec. 4 ), the HTA backbone has learned to extract features that distinguish one speaker from another. However, it learns them as a closed-set classifier, separating a fixed set of training speakers, whereas the deployed system faces an open-set problem. Its users are never part of training: a user is enrolled on the device from a short enrollment recording (Sec. 5.3 ), and no network weight is updated with that audio. In operation the device also hears guests who were never enrolled. The system must therefore recognise an enrolled speaker from a representation built from that recording and turn away audio from anyone else. Closed-set training exercises neither requirement: the classifier never builds a speaker representation from a few examples, and never encounters speakers outside its training set, whose voices may fall anywhere between the learned classes. Open-set recognition thus calls for an embedding extractor that has learned, from other speakers, how to separate speakers given only a few shots each, and how to separate them from speakers who are not enrolled. To this end, we propose the spiking embedding extractor (SEE), a 32-neuron spiking readout on top of the frozen backbone. The SEE is trained episodically on a disjoint speaker corpus: each episode enrolls a new set of training speakers from a few windows, identifies further windows of those speakers, and rejects speakers who are not enrolled, the same operations the deployed system later performs on its users without any further training. 5.1. The SEE is trained to produce embeddings for exactly these steps, so the network used at inference is the network trained, with no classifier or scoring layer added.
